section_title: Item 5A - Council Meeting 07/07/20206 (Second Public Hearing of City Charter Consideration)
text: Date: Sunday, July 5, 2026 7:48:20 PM Dear Mayor, Council member and City Manager, Thank you for the time and effort that the Council, Charter Advisory Committee, and City staff have invested in this important discussion. I have attended nearly every Charter Advisory Committee meeting, participated in the first public hearing, reviewed the staff reports and draft charter, and have continued following the discussion closely. Over the past several months, my perspective has evolved. Rather than focusing on whether Fremont should or should not become a Charter City, I have become more interested in ensuring that, if Fremont adopts a charter, it is one that is thoughtfully designed around Fremont's long-term needs. I also want to clarify that my primary concerns are not the recommendations regarding council compensation, benefits, or dedicated staff support. In my view, those are relatively small policy decisions in the context of a governing document that may shape Fremont for decades. Whether those items remain, are modified, or are removed does not fundamentally influence my view of the charter itself. Many of those items could also be considered under Fremont's existing General Law authority. Instead, my concerns are about the overall governance process and the long-term vision for the charter.

section_title: 2. Council Direction from the First Public Hearing
text: This is the second and final public hearing, yet the proposed charter remains subject to further revisions based on Council direction. The staff report itself requests additional direction on the proposed charter language before deciding whether to place it on the November 2026 ballot. From a transparency standpoint, I respectfully ask: How will residents have an opportunity to review and provide input on the final version of the charter before the Council decides whether to place it on the ballot? Since transparency and accountability have been identified as primary motivations for pursuing a charter, I believe the public should have an opportunity to review the final proposed document not only earlier drafts. During the June 2 hearing, the Council discussed several important principles, including: Transparency and accountability as a primary motivation for the charter. Clarification that the charter does not authorize a real property transfer tax. Clarification that future amendments to the charter would require voter approval. While I appreciate these discussions, I do not see all of these concepts clearly reflected in the draft charter itself. For example, if it is important to reassure residents that this charter does not authorize a real property transfer tax, would it not be more transparent to state that explicitly in the charter rather than relying on discussion during public hearings or language in a staff report?

The estimated one-time cost of placing this measure on the November 2026 ballot is between $610,690 and $854,966. Before making that investment of public funds, I believe residents would benefit from understanding how the Council will determine that the charter proposal is sufficiently complete, clearly understood, and adequately vetted by the community. Closing I remain open to the concept of a Charter City. I am not opposed to the idea itself. However, if Fremont is going to adopt what is effectively its local constitution, I believe we have a unique opportunity to create a model charter that reflects Fremont's specific needs and long-term vision not simply a collection of governance provisions that happen to exist in other charter cities. My hope is that the final charter presented to voters is one that residents understand, one that clearly addresses Fremont's needs, and one that Fremont can be proud of for decades to come. Thank you for your consideration, and I look forward to Tuesday's discussion. To: <rsalwan@fremont.gov>, <yazhang@fremont.gov>, <yshao@fremont.gov>, <tkeng@fremont.gov>, <dcampbell@fremont.gov>, <kkimberlin@fremont.gov>, <rliu@fremont.gov>, <kshackelford@fremont.gov>, <ralvarado@fremont.gov> Subject: Urgent Concerns Regarding the Revenue Measure Committee and Interference With a Council Priority Dear Mayor and Councilmembers, I am writing to raise serious concerns regarding the composition, leadership, and activities of the City’s revenue measure ad hoc committee. The ad hoc committee is led by the city manager and she is influencing the direction of that committee to undermine the Charter process. The charter initiative is not a peripheral issue. It has been identified as one of the City Council’s top three priorities. The Council has committed public time, resources, and significant community engagement to examining reforms intended to improve accountability, transparency, responsiveness, and the effectiveness of Fremont’s government. Despite that clear direction, several members of the revenue measure committee are openly and actively working against the charter measure. These individuals include Rick Jones, Dominic Dutra, Suzanne Chan, Bob Wieckwoski, and Bill Harrison who are simultaneously serving on a committee led by the City Manager while publicly advocating, organizing, or campaigning to defeat one of the Council’s highest priorities - the Charter initiative. There has also been some backchanneling and interference from Councilmember Kathy Kimberlin in this process. They are doing this by organizing meetings behind the scenes and coordinating a campaign to influence councilmembers to vote against the charter. They are also activating community members to speak in opposition of it at the next charter meeting. The City Manager heads the revenue measure ad hoc committee and exercised substantial influence over its membership. When individuals selected through that process then become active participants in an effort to undermine another major Council initiative—particularly a charter proposal that may affect the authority, oversight, and accountability of the City Manager—the appearance of institutional interference is unavoidable. I am deeply concerned that the authority of the City Manager’s office and the structure of the revenue committee may be being used to encourage, empower, or coordinate individuals who are attempting to derail the charter process. At a minimum, the circumstances create the public perception that the City Manager is using her position as head of the revenue committee to assemble or strengthen opposition to a Council-directed governance priority. That perception is deeply damaging, even if the activity is occurring outside official meetings. City staff are responsible for carrying out the policy direction of the elected Council. They should not use their official authority, control over appointments, access to community leaders, or influence over City-created committees to frustrate or sabotage priorities established by the Council. The concern is particularly acute because the charter proposal addresses the balance of power and accountability among the City Council, Mayor, City Manager, City Attorney, and senior administration. It is therefore reasonable for the Council and the public to question whether opposition from City Manager-selected committee members is truly independent or whether those members are being encouraged and influenced to protect the existing governance structure. This situation undermines the work of the charter committee and disrespects the residents who have devoted substantial time and effort to that process. It also risks sending a message that Council priorities can be quietly obstructed by administrative officials who disagree with them. In addition, this conduct could jeopardize the revenue measure itself. A revenue proposal will succeed only if the public trusts the people and process behind it. Residents may reasonably question why a committee formed to build community support for City services is populated by individuals who are simultaneously working to defeat and sabotage another formally established City priority. The City cannot credibly ask the public to support a revenue measure while allowing the committee promoting that measure to become a vehicle for opposition to the charter. I believe the Council should immediately request a full accounting of:

section_title: Item 5a: Charter - Political Consultant Catherine Lew working against Charter
text: Date: Monday, July 6, 2026 9:26:48 AM Dear Mayor and Councilmembers, I am writing because I believe we have a serious public trust issue that needs to be addressed directly and transparently regarding item 5A Charter City discussion. Two Big Concerns: Revenue Committee / Charter Opposition Concern: Several individuals selected for the City Manager’s revenue measure committee are also actively working against the charter measure, even though the charter is one of the City Council’s top priorities. This creates the appearance that a City-created process for one Council priority is being used, directly or indirectly, to undermine another Council priority focused on governance, accountability, and transparency. Poltical Consultant Conflict with Catherine Lew/ Political Network Concern: The more serious concern is that Catherine Lew and The Lew Edwards Group, who are connected to the revenue measure effort, are reportedly also helping organize opposition to the charter measure. If the same consultant network is working to pass the revenue measure while defeating the charter, it creates a serious public trust problem and raises the appearance that insiders are trying to secure new revenue while blocking reforms to City Hall accountability. Catherine Lew should step down. This is not about whether private residents have the right to support or oppose the charter. Of course they do. This is not about silencing anyone. This is about whether City-created processes, City-selected committees, City-connected consultants, and influential political relationships are being used in a way that undermines one of the Council’s highest priorities. The charter initiative is one of the top priorities of the Fremont City Council. The purpose is simple: to look at how Fremont governs itself and whether we can hold City Hall more accountable, responsive, transparent, and effective for residents. At the same time, the City is also exploring a revenue measure. That is also an important discussion. But these two efforts should not be working against each other. The concern is that several people connected to the City Manager’s revenue committee are now actively working against the charter. These are not random residents. These are individuals selected because they are influential, recognizable, and politically connected in Fremont. They were brought into a City Manager-led process to advise on one possible ballot measure, and now some of those same individuals are helping organize opposition to another Council priority. The reason they claim they are doing that is because if we put both measures on the charter, both will fail and they really want to get more money. To the average resident, that does not look clean. It looks like insiders working behind the scenes. Even if no one was formally instructed to oppose the charter, the appearance is still troubling. City Hall should not create a situation where people selected for one City effort appear to be using their access, relationships, and credibility to defeat another City effort. This concern becomes even more serious because the charter measure deals directly with governance, accountability, and the balance of authority between the Council, Mayor, City Manager, City Attorney, and senior staff. When a measure could affect how power is distributed at City Hall, any opposition connected to City management, City-selected committees, or City-connected consultants deserves extra scrutiny. There is also a concern involving the consultant connected to the revenue measure. Catherine Lew and The Lew Edwards Group are paid as political consultants for the revenue measure effort. At the same time, Catherine Lew is reportedly involved in organizing or assisting opposition to the charter measure. She has also previously worked as a political consultant and confidant for former Councilmembers Sue Chan and Dominic Dutra, who are now being associated with last-minute opposition to the charter. That raises an obvious question: are the same political relationships being used to help pass the revenue measure while defeating the charter? It may appear that the revenue measure is being protected while the charter is being undermined. It may appear that influential insiders want the City to ask residents for more money, but do not want residents to have a real conversation about reforming how City Hall operates. It may appear that the political network around the revenue measure wants the revenue measure to succeed and the charter to fail. That perception is harmful to both measures. If residents believe the revenue measure is connected to an effort to defeat governance reform, they may lose trust in the revenue measure. If residents believe the charter is being opposed by insiders who benefit from the current system, they may lose trust in City Hall. Either way, the City loses. The bigger issue is influence, access, relationships, timing, consultant involvement, and public perception. Why are members of a City Manager-selected revenue committee actively opposing a top Council priority? Why is a consultant connected to the revenue measure also reportedly involved in organizing opposition to the charter? Why are former elected officials with prior consultant relationships being mobilized at the last minute against the charter? Why was the Council not clearly informed about these overlapping roles and relationships? What safeguards exist to make sure one City effort is not being used to defeat another? These are fair questions. The City should not dismiss these concerns as false or damaging. What damages public trust is not the act of asking questions. What damages public trust is when City Hall appears defensive instead of transparent. You should be able to say clearly and publicly that no City resources, City-funded consultants, City-created committees, City contact lists, City information, or City relationships are being used to oppose the charter. You should also be able to say that anyone involved in the revenue measure effort is fully separated from any anticharter campaign activity. Right now, I do not believe those safeguards have been clearly established. At a minimum, I believe the Council should request the following:

Respectfully, Ray Rodriguez 47+ year proud Fremont resident From: Anu Natarajan To: councilmeetings Subject: A Flawed Process Undermines even Potentially Good Ideas Date: Monday, July 6, 2026 10:36:48 AM Dear Mayor and Councilmembers, I have not come before the Fremont City Council since completing my 10-year tenure as a vice mayor/councilmember. I have great respect for the responsibility of serving on the dais, the complexity of local government, and the difficult decisions you are asked to make on behalf of our community. But I felt compelled to speak up on this issue because the decision before you is different. A city charter is not another policy initiative. It is the foundation for how Fremont governs itself. It defines the relationship between residents and their local government and could shape decision-making for generations. A decision of this magnitude requires a process that matches its importance. Unfortunately, I do not believe the process to date has met that standard. My concern is not about whether Fremont should ever explore becoming a charter city. Cities should evolve. Governance structures should be examined. We should always look for ways to improve how government serves residents. My concern is that we started with a solution before we clearly defined the problem. For the past several years, my work has focused on systems change — helping communities tackle complex challenges by bringing together government, residents, nonprofits, philanthropy, and the private sector around shared solutions. The most important lesson from that work is simple: You cannot create lasting change without trust. And you cannot build trust without authentic engagement. Authentic civic engagement is not asking residents to react to a proposal after it has already been developed. It is not a public hearing where people have two minutes at a microphone after decisions are already moving forward. True engagement begins much earlier. It starts by educating the community, creating a shared understanding of the challenges, bringing diverse voices to the table, defining the problem together, and then identifying the best solutions. The questions residents are asking today should have been the starting point: What problem are we solving? Why is a charter city the right solution? What can we accomplish as a charter city that we cannot accomplish today? What are the measurable outcomes for residents? How will this make Fremont a stronger, more effective, more responsive city? Instead, we are now considering moving toward the ballot after a compressed process that has left many residents only beginning to understand what is being proposed. That should concern all of us. The strongest ideas are not weakened by public engagement. They are strengthened by it. If becoming a charter city is truly the right path for Fremont, then taking the time to build understanding, trust, and community ownership will only result in a better outcome. I would also encourage the Council to think about the long-term precedent this decision creates. Governance reform should always be designed for the institution and the residents it serves — not for a particular moment in time or the individuals currently holding office. That is why a more thoughtful process matters. I respectfully ask the Council to pause this effort, step back from the current timeline, and restart next year with an authentic community engagement process. Start with residents. Start with education. Start with the question: What kind of government does Fremont need for the next generation? Then decide whether a charter is the right tool. The measure of good government is not how quickly we make decisions. It is whether the community trusts the decisions we make. Fremont has always been a city shaped by engaged residents, innovation, and collaboration. Let's honor that tradition and ensure that a decision this important is developed through a process worthy of the community it will serve. Respectfully, Anu Natarajan From: Shakira Karipineni To: Raj Salwan; councilmeetings Subject: Slow Down the Charter City Process and Engage the Community Date: Monday, July 6, 2026 3:14:35 PM In the name of God Dear Honorable Mayor and Councilmembers, I am writing to express my opposition to moving forward with the proposed Charter City initiative at this time. A city charter is the equivalent of a local constitution. Before asking voters to approve a charter, the City should clearly answer four questions:

section_title: 1. What problem are we trying to solve? / 2. Why can't it be solved under the current system? / 3. What are the anticipated costs? / 4. How will residents benefit?
text: Until those questions are answered, I urge the Council to pause the process and invest in broader community engagement. Good governance requires transparency, trust, and public participation. Fremont deserves nothing less. Sincerely, Shakira Karipineni Fremont Resident From: David Bonaccorsi To: councilmeetings Cc: kshakelford@fremont.gov; Rafael E. Alvarado, Jr. Subject: 7/7 Agenda Item 5A: No on Charter: Not Now! Not This Way! Date: Monday, July 6, 2026 4:18:45 PM Dear Honorable Mayor and Members of the Fremont City Council. While you know I have commented at great length on Facebook and NextDoor why I am opposed to placing a Charter initiative on the November ballot, at this time, and in this way (and I encourage those of you who have not read my posts to do so), I will augment and crystallize what I have been articulating over the past several days on social media. You now have the opportunity at the Council Chambers in public to ask staff or address in comments before taking action on 7/7 and at any time before the Council takes action (if it does) on placing the Charter in final form before the 7/28 deadline for a vote on the November ballot. Section 800 of the proposed charter is entitled “Compliance with State law”. Section 800 states in relevant part that “This Charter shall comply with the Constitution of the State of California, and any provisions herein that may conflict with state law shall be deemed superseded by the applicable statutes.” (Bold italics added). So, members of the Council who support placing this measure on the ballot have an obligation to let us know which provisions if any of this proposed Charter do not conflict with State law – or have the City Attorney in his presentation on this matter, specify which provisions do not conflict with State law. The questions respectfully I would like to hear from members of the Council in light of Section 800 are, as follows: What is exactly the Council attempting to accomplish as a Charter City that cannot be accomplished already as a general law City? So, the next question should be: Which provisions of the Charter are consistent with our State Constitution and State law which are already allowed as a general law city such that we don’t even need a Charter to enact or carry forward these provisions? For example, Fremont doesn’t need a Charter to have our residents vote on extending the Mayor and Councilmember terms (or the terms of a future Mayor and Councilmember)s from two term limits to three. That can be placed on the ballot as a stand alone measure without being part of the package deal for a Charter initiative. Let’s have that debate. Proposed Section 404, subdivisions (d) in the Charter states “Time spent in office while serving less than a full term shall not be counted in computing consecutive years in office.” What does that mean for any Councilmember who is otherwise termed out and not otherwise eligible to run in November? Likely that Councilmember would not be eligible, but I am not advising the Council as an attorney – that’s the role of your City Attorney. That discussion should be made part of the public record. More importantly, the Council or staff should make clear whether Section 404 would allow any incumbents to the City Council to run for 12 more years regardless of their years of service to date. And why the Council should not eliminate Section 404 subdivisions (d) and (e) or make it apply only to members of the Council who: (1) have yet to be elected to Council; or (2) to existing members of the Council who would honor the existing term limits of two terms and sit out at least one 4-year election cycle and then run again to be eligible to run at that time for three successive 4-year terms. Why do we need an “independent” City Attorney as proclaimed on social media? Independent of whom? The City Attorney already serves at the pleasure of the City Council and would continue to do so if this Charter is approved by the voters. Section 700 and Section 701 of the proposed Charter seemingly carries forward the powers and duties that exist in Fremont already as a general law city. How does the Charter alter the City Attorney’s powers and duties? Under what circumstances without voter approval can the office of the City Attorney become an elected position? By a simple ordinance? Apparently, the City of Fremont does need a Charter to increase your salaries and increase staffing as proposed in this Charter. Section 406 of the proposed Charter does authorize (after the Charter has been approved by the voters) changing the salary structure of the Council at Council’s own discretion by ordinance. And doing so after without going back to the voters for any pay raises or increased staffing. Section 406 has limiting language but is not legally binding. Section 406 states that the Council shall “take into consideration a survey of comparable cities within the region.” Who defines the “region”? Who defines what are “comparable cities”? Who performs the “survey”? Who hires the consultant or consultants to perform the survey? Are the results of the survey shared with the public in an agendized hearing before an increase in salaries is perhaps put on the consent calendar? To be clearly transparent, the Council if it places this ballot on the measure should indicate that there is nothing that binds the Council to the results of its own survey. The Council can ignore the survey and can propose a higher salary limited only by the ability to get 4 votes on Council. A Charter is like the Constitution for our City. I’ve made clear that, unlike others perhaps, I am not opposed to having a conversation about considering after 70 years how we govern ourselves. But process matters. And in that spirit, I do believe the Vice Mayor initiated this discussion by way of her referral in good faith. And because it is like a Constitution for our City, historical analogies to the adoption of the U.S. Constitution are in order to compare it with our truncated, superficial process. No, we don’t need only scholars or attorneys on the Advisory Committee. But, with some notable exceptions, including former Councilmember Rick Jones who served the advisory committee admirably, the measure of their service is not the value of their time (which I do not diminish in the least), but in the level of experience and understanding of the nuance of local governance far more than they could ever hope to bring to the table. 6 meetings for a couple of hours as a volunteer are not enough meetings to grasp what it means to be a general law city or a charter city, much less engage in the higher-level deliberation of comparing and contrasting the advantages and disadvantages of being a general law versus a charter city. I spent 12 years combined on Planning Commission and City Council (and two years previously on another advisory committee). I was appointed by the late former Mayor Gus Morrison to serve to Chair an oversight committee supervising the dissolution of Fremont’s redevelopment agency (RDA) composed of representatives appointed by various local taxing agencies impacted by the RDA dismantling. These members elected me as their Chair. I can say with integrity that I only fully appreciated what it means to be a general law city in the two years I was privileged to serve on the City Council with direct contact with the City Manager and interaction with the heads of various departments throughout the City. A better process for a re-start of the Charter initiative would be to replicate what was done in the 90s when the City last placed a charter initiative on the ballot. Each councilmember was able to appoint two members to the Charter Commission, and this Commission spent a year convening regularly (and I believe advised by a consultant and certainly qualified City staff) before proposing a charter for Council consideration. That Commission was headed by David Lanferman, a Mission San High graduate who at the time had a law practice in Fremont and was highly respected as an attorney and a member of the community citywide. The members of that Charter Commission didn’t agree with each other as they reflected the diverse views of the Councilmembers and Mayor who appointed the advisory commissioners. So, they spent time forging compromise after high level deliberations and had enough time over that year to become subject matter experts on what it meant to be a charter versus a general law city. We need a year at least to engage the public conducting multiple town hall meetings comparable and greater than the City conducted during the selection of the Housing Navigation Center which was supposed to be just a 3-year temporary shelter alternative. That there were press releases generally from the City and 6 meetings and a timeline going back to a referral in February, or even to a Council retreat, are not substitutes for the full-fledged, full court outreach for engaging the broader public on such an important and foundational issue of how we govern ourselves in Fremont that is intended to be permanent. And by analogy to the adoption of our Constitution, there was not a 10-week campaign with glossy mailers and messaging by highly paid political consultants to try to “wow” the citizens of the United States to urge their legislators in the 13 states to ratify the Constitution. A campaign for the Charter from dropping of the ballot in late August to early voting just weeks later in early October is where facts and a meaningful dialogue will go to die. The residents will be subjected to campaign slogans like “local control” as some sort of talismanic panacea and a one-size-fits-all solution to all of our challenges as a City. Contrast that with the ratification of our U.S. Constitution. Madison, Hamilton, and John Jay (who later became the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court) over a period of a year published in local newspapers of the day the Federalist Papers. The Federalist Papers educated and informed the citizens of the United States why this new Constitution needed to be adopted. And the drafters also listened to the citizens who were concerned with governmental overreach. That is why they pivoted and added the Bill of Rights as the First 10 Amendments to curb and limit federal power that needed to be reserved expressly to the States and to the people. We in Fremont are highly educated but most of us don’t hang on press releases posted on the City website, attend advisory committee meetings, or even know such meetings exist. I don’t want to stop a conversation. There has been no meaningful conversation to stop as it has never even begun. I am respectfully encouraging you to start the conversation the right way. And to have a dialogue where the Fremont City Council listen to the concerns of all voters not just the few appointed to a 6-week advisory commission or who happen to already learn about this Charter process. This process has been too much of an inside baseball rollout only for the few who are already in the know. We need a process that respects the intelligence of all our residents in Fremont. We can and must do better. David P. Bonaccorsi, Esq. Duncan Resident of Fremont since 1990 From: Jagadeesh Ginjupalli To: councilmeetings; Raj Salwan; Raymond Liu; Teresa Keng; Desrie Campbell; Kathy Kimberlin; Yang Shao; Yajing Zhang Subject: Support for Accepting the Charter Advisory Committee Recommendations Date: Monday, July 6, 2026 8:13:01 PM Dear Mayor and City Council Members, I am writing this email to express my strong support for accepting the Charter Advisory Committee's recommendations and advancing the proposed City Charter. The Charter Advisory Committee devoted significant time and effort in studying this important issue, listening to public input, and developing thoughtful recommendations for the City Council. I appreciate the Council's commitment to a transparent public process and careful consideration of the Committee's work. Accepting the Charter Advisory Committee's recommendations and moving the proposed City Charter forward will provide Fremont City with greater local control over municipal affairs, increased flexibility to address local needs, and the opportunity for Fremont voters to decide this important question in the November 2026 election. section_title: Item 5A: No on Charter! No! Not Now! No! Not This Way!
text: Date: Tuesday, July 7, 2026 11:24:10 AM Dear City Council, A Charter is a new Constitution for our City when we have been a general law city for 70 years since our city first became a city in 1956. On July 4, we celebrated our 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. But it took 11 years before we had our Constitution after a months long Constitutional convention. The Constitution - the Charter for the U.S. - was adopted only after our country first screwed up with the Articles of Confederation that didn’t work. Don’t let Fremont screw it up with this Charter, this way, at this time. No, not now, and not this way. Our U.S. Constitution gathered the best minds of the country for days on end to hash out a document for the ages at a constitutional convention. In Fremont, the Council created our own Charter convention, the Fremont Charter Advisory Commission. They did not meet daily, but weekly, and only just 6 times! But the Fremont Charter Advisory Commission - with just a few exceptions (unlike our Constitutional Convention that met in Philly) - did not include talented people who applied but were rejected who actually understood how local government works. There was no James Madison or Ben Franklin among them on this Fremont Charter Advisory Commission. They couldn’t even agree among themselves how to select their own chair. This Advisory Commission was leaderless and rudderless where Fremont’s best and brightest need not apply. I’m not saying never Charter (even though others may say no, not now and never needed). I am saying not now and not this way as this process had as much thoughtful consideration as sweeping right on a dating app! We need more and better input from all of us in Fremont and not have this rushed through as some sort of pet project for a few hoping no one notices. Alvarado, Jr. Subject: Public Comment: Council Meeting July 7, 2026 Agenda Item 5A – Second Public Hearing Charter Proposal Request Improvment On Public Comment Procedures and Meeting Decorum Date: Tuesday, July 7, 2026 12:54:36 PM Dear Mayor Salwan, Vice Mayor Zhang, and Councilmembers, As the City Council prepares to conduct the second public hearing regarding the proposed Fremont City Charter, I respectfully request that the Council exercise its discretion to maximize meaningful public participation and ensure consistent enforcement of meeting decorum during the Public Hearing portion of Agenda Item 5A. While the Brown Act does not prescribe a fixed speaking time for public comment, Government Code 54954.3 authorizes legislative bodies to adopt reasonable regulations governing the time, place, and manner of public comment. At the same time, Government Code 54950 declares that the Brown Act exists to ensure that the people's business is conducted openly and that the public remains informed so that it may retain control over the instruments of government it has created. The proposed charter language for tonight's discussion is not an ordinary legislative item. If adopted, it will become Fremont's foundational governing document and may define the City's governmental structure for decades. Given the exceptional institutional significance of this proposal, I encourage the Council to allow up to three minutes per speaker during Agenda

section_title: Item 5A rather than a time reduction should attendance exceed expectations. While
text: abbreviated time limits may be appropriate for routine matters, a municipal charter warrants broader public participation whenever feasible. This request is not based upon any assertion that the Brown Act requires additional speaking time. Rather, I am asking the Council to exercise the discretion already afforded under state law in a manner consistent with the transparency and accountability objectives repeatedly cited throughout the charter initiative itself. I also respectfully request consistent, content-neutral enforcement of the meeting decorum throughout tonight's hearing. Audience demonstrations including prolonged applause, booing, shouting, chanting, or other audible interruptions can interfere with speakers, discourage or chill participation by members of the public, and detract from thoughtful deliberation when they materially disrupt the orderly conduct of the meeting. Fremont is also home to a diverse demographic where public commenters may be communicating English as a second language and require additional time to formulate their thoughts, making any extemporaneous interruptions an impediment to legally entitled civic engagement. More specifically, I observed intermittent decorum issues at previous Council meetings on June 16 and May 12, where outbursts were only addressed after the fact and would appreciate improvements from those meetings. Both state and federal courts have recognized that legislative bodies possess authority to regulate public meetings through reasonable, viewpoint-neutral rules designed to preserve order while protecting the public's right to participate. In White v. City of Norwalk (1990) 900 F.2d 1421, the Ninth Circuit explained that procedural rules governing public comment are permissible when directed toward preventing actual disruption rather than suppressing particular viewpoints. More recently, in Berkeley People's Alliance v. City of Berkeley (2025) 114 Cal.App.5th 984, the California Court of Appeal reaffirmed that exceptions to the Brown Act's open meeting requirements must be narrowly construed because the Act is intended to maximize public participation in local government decision-making. Accordingly, while the Council retains discretion to establish reasonable procedures governing public comment, I encourage the Council to exercise that discretion in favor of broader public participation during consideration of a proposed municipal charter. A city charter is among the most consequential governance decisions a city can present to its electorate, and where reasonable discretion exists, it should be exercised in a manner that promotes, rather than limits, meaningful public participation. Accordingly, I respectfully request that any rules governing speaking time and audience conduct be applied uniformly regardless of whether a participant supports or opposes the proposed charter. Consistent enforcement of existing decorum rules promotes fairness, protects every speaker's opportunity to be heard, and reinforces public confidence in the integrity of the Council's proceedings. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Henry Soong
